Title: Diagnosis of test `testIsSameLocalTime_Cal()`

Details:
The test `testIsSameLocalTime_Cal()` fails due to the incorrect behavior of the method `DateUtils.isSameLocalTime(Calendar, Calendar)`.

Examining the method `DateUtils.isSameLocalTime`, we see the following implementation:

```java
public static boolean isSameLocalTime(Calendar cal1, Calendar cal2) {
    if (cal1 == null || cal2 == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("The date must not be null");
    }
    return (cal1.get(Calendar.MILLISECOND) == cal2.get(Calendar.MILLISECOND) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.SECOND) == cal2.get(Calendar.SECOND) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.MINUTE) == cal2.get(Calendar.MINUTE) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.HOUR) == cal2.get(Calendar.HOUR) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.DAY_OF_YEAR) == cal2.get(Calendar.DAY_OF_YEAR) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.YEAR) == cal2.get(Calendar.YEAR) &&
            cal1.get(Calendar.ERA) == cal2.get(Calendar.ERA) &&
            cal1.getClass() == cal2.getClass());
}
```

The main issue is the comparison on line 265: `cal1.get(Calendar.HOUR) == cal2.get(Calendar.HOUR)`. The `Calendar.HOUR` field is the hour in 12-hour clock format (0-11). This causes problematic results when the two calendar instances have the same hour of the day in 24-hour format (`Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY`) but differ in AM/PM, or when clocks are set at different times in the same 12-hour period with different time zones.

For example, in the test, the two calendars `cal3` and `cal4` are set as:

```java
cal3.set(2004, 6, 9, 4, 0, 0);  // 4 AM
cal4.set(2004, 6, 9, 16, 0, 0); // 4 PM
```

Both have the same `Calendar.HOUR` value (4), but represent different times of day (because one is in AM, the other in PM). Since the code compares only `Calendar.HOUR` (12-hour clock) but not `Calendar.AM_PM`, the method may incorrectly return true for times that represent different local times.

One would expect the test to return `false` (as the assertion expects), recognizing these as different local times (4:00 AM vs 4:00 PM), but the broken logic on the `HOUR` field alone may cause incorrect behavior.

The fix is to replace the comparison of `Calendar.HOUR` with `Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY`, which is the 24-hour clock hour (0-23), fully representing the hour of the day unambiguously.

Additionally, the test sets milliseconds to zero which is appropriate, so millisecond differences don't affect.

Summary:
- The bug stems from comparing `Calendar.HOUR` (12-hour clock) instead of `Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY` (24-hour clock).
- This leads to false positives in comparisons where times differ by AM/PM but match in `Calendar.HOUR`.
- The failing test identified this by setting 4 AM and 4 PM, which have the same `Calendar.HOUR` but different `Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY`.

Recommended fix locations:
- `org.apache.commons.lang3.time.DateUtils.isSameLocalTime(java.util.Calendar,java.util.Calendar)` should be modified to use `Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY` instead of `Calendar.HOUR`.
org.apache.commons.lang3.time.DateUtils.isSameLocalTime(java.util.Calendar,java.util.Calendar)
